title: Bach
objective: After this level you can describe Bach's music and why musicians revere it.
summary: Bach (1685 to 1750) was admired in his lifetime mainly as an organist. His fugues and The Well-Tempered Clavier, and Mendelssohn's 1829 St. Matthew Passion, made him the composer musicians revere.

cards.headline: When Bach died, people remembered a great organist.
cards.body: Johann Sebastian Bach ran the church music in Leipzig from 1723 until his death in 1750. In his lifetime he was admired mainly as a brilliant harpsichordist, organist and organ expert. Today he is regarded as one of the greatest composers in history. What did the world miss, and how did it find him again?

cards.headline: A fugue: one theme, many voices
cards.body: Bach's specialty was the fugue. One voice states a main theme, called the subject. Then a second voice enters with the same theme while the first keeps going, then a third, until several lines weave together, each taking its turn with the subject. It works a little like singing a round, but with far more freedom. Britannica calls Bach's fugues unsurpassed in variety and perfection, written for every medium he had.

mascot.line: Try following one voice through a fugue while the others keep talking. Hard at first, then strangely addictive.

cards.fact: Bach wrote a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key.
cards.context: The Well-Tempered Clavier comes in two books, the first from 1722, and each holds 24 preludes and fugues. Why 24? Remember Level 8: Western keyboards split the octave into 12 equal semitones. Put a major key and a minor key on each of those 12 notes and you get 24. Bach visited every one, twice.

cards.headline: The comeback: Berlin, 1829
cards.body: The turning point came on March 11, 1829, in Berlin, when 20-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion, its first performance since Bach died. It launched a 19th-century Bach revival that never really ended. The organist Leipzig remembered became the composer musicians revere.

cards.headline: Bach: revered
learned: Bach led Leipzig's church music from 1723 to 1750
In his day he was admired mainly as an organist
A fugue passes one subject from voice to voice
Mendelssohn's 1829 St. Matthew Passion revived him

questions.prompt: In one of Bach's fugues, what is the subject?

options.label: The words the choir sings
options.rationale: A fugue's subject is a musical theme, not a text.

options.label: The main theme each voice takes up in turn
The final chord that ends the piece
options.rationale: The subject opens the fugue and keeps returning.

options.label: The bass line the harpsichord improvises on

questions.explanation: A fugue's subject is its main theme, stated by one voice and then imitated by each of the others.

questions.prompt: What did Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St. Matthew Passion do for Bach's reputation?

options.label: It premiered a Bach piece nobody had written down
options.rationale: The Passion was Bach's own finished work.

options.label: It launched a revival of Bach's music
It proved Bach had been a great organist
options.rationale: That was already how he was remembered.

options.label: It marked the 100th anniversary of his death
options.rationale: Bach died in 1750, only 79 years earlier.

questions.explanation: It was the Passion's first performance since Bach's death, and it launched the 19th-century Bach revival.

questions.prompt: Why does each book of The Well-Tempered Clavier hold 24 preludes and fugues?

options.label: One for each hour of the day
options.rationale: The number comes from keys, not the clock.

options.label: 12 notes, each with a major and a minor key
Two for each note of the major scale
options.rationale: The major scale has 7 notes, which gives 14.

questions.explanation: Twelve semitones in the octave, each starting a major key and a minor key, make 24 keys.
